title: From AI experiments to AI-native hospitals
thbAction: Position THB's pharma CRM and omnichannel HCP engagement workflows to support launch planning, KAM orchestration, and compliant follow-up across India and the Middle East.
contentHtml:
AI Diagnostics CXO Leadership Forum, organised by ETHealthworld in association with 5C Network is bringing together leading experts to find out what it will take to scale.Artificial intelligence (AI) has moved from discussion rooms into hospital corridors. It is being used to assist clinicians, support diagnostics and improve operational workflows. The bigger story now is execution, not adoption. Why do some healthcare organisations succeed in embedding AI across their systems while others remain stuck in the trial phase?

The pattern is consistent across the hospitals that have actually made the jump: the ones that scale treat AI as a workflow decision, not a procurement decision. The ones that stall buy a tool and hand it to IT. Scaling hospitals redesign the process itself, deciding who reviews what, in what order, with what sign-off, and let the AI take its place inside that redesigned process.

Advt

The question has gained urgency as India's healthcare sector enters a new growth phase. Demand for healthcare services continues to rise, driven by an ageing population, greater insurance penetration and a growing burden of chronic diseases. According to an industry report cited by The Economic Times, India's hospital market reached $193.4 billion in FY25 and is projected to grow to $364.6 billion by 2034. For hospitals, growth is no longer simply about adding beds or opening new facilities. The ability to improve productivity, manage rising patient volumes and support clinical teams more effectively is becoming equally important.

These are among the issues that will be discussed at the inaugural AI Diagnostics CXO Leadership Forum, organised by ETHealthworld in association with 5C Network on October 9 in New Delhi. Positioned as an invitation-only gathering for healthcare decision-makers, it aims to examine how intelligent diagnostics and AI can move beyond technology deployments to become drivers of institutional growth.

Why scaling AI remains difficultMany hospitals can point to a successful AI deployment, whether in radiology, pathology or hospital operations. Scaling those gains across an organisation, however, remains a tougher proposition. Which raises a question occupying healthcare boardrooms: what separates a hospital that scales from one that stalls?

Advt

Radiology answers this most clearly, because it was the first clinical domain where the redesign question could not be avoided. High imaging volume and structured, measurable outcomes forced hospitals to either rebuild the reporting workflow around AI or leave it as a side project. Platforms like 5C Network now process over 20,000 radiology reports a day across more than 2,000 hospital partners, and that scale exists precisely because the workflow was rebuilt rather than layered with a tool.

Radiology has proven the model works. It has not yet proven that the model travels. Adoption across most other departments, and across most hospitals outside the leading tier, remains at an early stage, and the gap between what a handful of innovators have built and what the rest of the market is doing is still wide. That gap is the more useful problem for this forum to address than the original question of whether AI works at all.

Advt

For CXOs shaping the next generation of healthcare enterprises, the answer extends beyond technology. Investment choices, clinician buy-in, operational readiness and the ability to generate measurable returns all play a role. These issues will be at the centre of conversation at this upcoming forum, where hospital CEOs, diagnostics leaders, technology innovators and investors will examine how intelligent diagnostics are moving from a support function to a strategic contributor to hospital growth.Few areas illustrate AI's promise quite like diagnostics. Hospitals are handling larger volumes of scans and tests than ever before, often with limited specialist capacity. In that environment, AI is being used to help clinicians prioritise cases, interpret findings and improve reporting efficiency. That shift is already visible at scale in Indian radiology, where AI-assisted reporting now runs across thousands of hospitals rather than isolated pilot sites.

For healthcare providers, the conversation has therefore become less about technology acquisition and more about execution. Questions around clinical adoption, governance, accountability and integration are now moving closer to the centre of decision-making. Radiology's experience shows what responsible deployment at scale actually requires: clear sign-off protocols, defined accountability between the AI system and the reporting clinician, and integration into the existing reporting workflow rather than around it. Today's debate is less about whether AI works and more about how hospitals can integrate it into day-to-day operations, extend it across departments, and convert innovation into measurable value.That question of spread, rather than proof, is where the classic theory of diffusion of innovation is useful, but it also requires being honest about what the early adopters actually went through. The hard part of early AI radiology deployment was rarely cost. It was learning how to make the technology work inside a real reporting environment, with real radiologists, under real time pressure. Much of that learning was uncomfortable. Radiologists had to work through a genuine unsettling of their role, at a time when AI was frequently measured against the best possible human reading rather than against the baseline it was actually meant to support. That comparison set an unfair and often misleading bar, and it took time for departments to recognise it as such.The more durable lesson to emerge from that period is that AI in radiology is not a finished capability that a hospital either buys or does not. It is a system that improves with use, feedback, and correction, and its value compounds incrementally rather than arriving all at once. Early adopters who understood this treated the first deployment as the start of a learning curve, not the end of one. Hospitals now entering the space do not need to relive that curve from the beginning. What they need is a clear account of it: how radiologists' concerns were addressed rather than dismissed, how expectations were reset once AI was judged against the right benchmark, and how value was allowed to accumulate over successive rounds of use rather than demanded on day one. The forum is built around exactly that transfer, using the experience of innovators and early adopters in radiology and diagnostics to give the wider market a faster, lower-risk path to the same outcome.Healthcare organisations are converging on one practical question above the rest: how should ROI be measured? The clearest signal is not cost saved per scan but specialist time reclaimed. When AI-assisted triage shortens turnaround on high-priority cases, the return shows up as faster clinical decisions and fewer bottlenecks upstream of radiology, not simply cheaper reporting.The said event will serve as a platform to find such answers. Bringing together hospital CEOs, CIOs, CMOs, medical directors, diagnostics leaders and business heads, it is designed for decision-makers responsible for shaping healthcare strategy, operations and technology adoption. Discussions will centre on implementation experiences, investment priorities and the practical realities of scaling AI across health systems.Building hospitals that can scale intelligentlyMany healthcare organisations now view AI as part of a broader operating model rather than a collection of stand-alone tools. The idea behind the AI-native hospital is not that every process becomes automated. Rather, intelligence is embedded where it can improve decision-making, efficiency and patient care.Leadership teams are evaluating technology through the lens of long-term business performance rather than short-term experimentation. Investment trends also point to AI's growing role across health systems. According to industry forecasts, the global AI healthcare market is expected to exceed $90 billion by 2030, driven by demand for AI-powered diagnostics, predictive analytics and workflow optimisation tools.Market forecasts may be impressive, but hospital boards tend to judge success differently. Patient outcomes, operational efficiency and clinician acceptance remain the measures that matter. At AI Diagnostics CXO Leadership Forum, these priorities are expected to shape the exchange of real-life and practical frameworks among leaders from hospitals, diagnostics and healthcare technology. For C-suite executives steering the future of healthcare, this exclusive event will offer a close look at the strategies, investments and real-world lessons through six high-impact sessions.As hospitals expand their AI ambitions, the challenge is shifting from experimentation to execution. The hospitals that treat AI as infrastructure, not experiment, will set the pace for the next phase of healthcare delivery. Radiology has shown what that looks like at scale, but the innovators who got there first are still the exception rather than the norm.
